opus-5.5.text:
I think it happened gradually, and honestly more through results than through arguments.

When I started, a lot of people in robotics, including in our lab, came from a very classical background: planning, control, optimization, careful modeling of the system. That tradition is powerful. If you can write down the physics and the constraints, you can get guarantees and behavior you understand. So there was a healthy skepticism toward learning. People would ask, "Why would I learn something I could just model?" or "How do I know this neural network won't do something crazy on the real robot?"

What changed things was running into problems where modeling just didn't scale. Manipulation is the classic example. Contact is messy, objects are deformable, friction is hard to estimate, and the world is full of things you didn't anticipate. You can spend months hand-engineering a pipeline for one task, and then a slightly different object or lighting condition breaks it. At some point people started to feel that pain directly in their own projects.

Then a few demonstrations, from our lab and from the broader community, showed that a learned policy, sometimes trained from a modest amount of human demonstration data, could handle variation that the hand-designed system couldn't. Once you see a robot do something robustly that you struggled with for a long time, it's hard to argue with.

But I'd say the acceptance wasn't "machine learning replaces everything." It was more that learning became one tool that sits alongside the classical tools. The people with the strongest robotics intuition were often the ones who used learning best, because they knew where structure helps: what to model explicitly, what to leave to data, how to design the action space, how to evaluate honestly on hardware. A lot of the productive conversations in the lab were about that combination rather than one camp winning.

There's also a cultural part. Students talk to each other. When one person gets a learning-based approach working and shares the code, the data-collection setup, the tricks, other people try it on their problems. It spreads through the lab almost like a practice, not just an idea.

And I think we're still in that process. There are open questions about data, about generalization, about safety and reliability that the classical side keeps pushing on, and I think that tension is actually good for the field.

r001.rationale: The response says acceptance grew through results and demonstrations, including seeing a learned policy handle variation robustly where hand-designed systems struggled.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning alongside classical tools and learned policies, but does not describe a shift from perception within manually planned workflows to robots learning motion paths.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. Honestly, it wasn't a clean conversion. When I started, our lab was very much a classical robotics group: everything was models, kinematics, carefully tuned controllers. The attitude toward learning was skeptical, and I'd say rightly so, because the early demos we saw were fragile. A policy would work on one table with one lighting setup and fall apart the moment you moved the camera.

What changed it was less a single breakthrough and more a slow accumulation of embarrassment, if I can put it that way. We kept running into perception problems that our hand-engineered pipelines simply couldn't handle. Grasping cluttered, deformable, or partially occluded objects was the big one. We'd spend months tuning a feature detector, and then a student would train a network over a weekend and get better results on the same test set. That happened enough times that even the most skeptical senior people started asking, okay, where else does this apply?

The second thing was that learning stopped being an all-or-nothing proposal. Once we framed it as, keep the controller, keep the planner, but let a learned model handle the messy perception part, or let it estimate the parameters that were previously hand-set, it became much easier to accept. Nobody had to throw away their expertise. It was a tool that plugged into the existing stack.

And the third piece, which I think people underrate, was infrastructure. Learning only became practical once we had decent data collection, simulation that was good enough to pretrain in, and the compute to iterate quickly. Before that, every experiment was so expensive that one failure would set the whole idea back for months.

So by the end it wasn't really that the lab decided machine learning was the right philosophy. It was that the results became impossible to ignore, and the integration became low enough risk that trying it was the rational thing to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says a student trained a network that outperformed the hand-engineered approach on the same test set, and that repeated results shifted skeptical lab members toward acceptance.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes learning for perception and parameter estimation within the existing robotics stack, but does not say the robot learned motion paths itself.

astra-6.text: I think it was a gradual process. In robotics, people want to see whether an approach actually works on the robot. So machine learning gains acceptance when it solves a problem that’s been difficult to solve by hand, and when that result holds up beyond a single demonstration. I’d describe it less as everyone suddenly deciding that learning was the answer, and more as building confidence through those practical successes. You start to see where learning helps, where you still need structure, and how the two can work together.

r001.rationale: It says machine learning gains acceptance when it solves difficult problems on the robot and builds confidence through practical successes.

r002.rationale: It does not describe a shift from perception in a manually planned workflow to the robot learning motion paths itself.

sol-6.1.text: I think it was a gradual process. In robotics, people want to see that a method works on the actual robot, where there’s noise and uncertainty and things don’t behave exactly as they do in simulation. So the most convincing argument for machine learning was demonstrating that it could solve a problem that was difficult to handle with our existing methods. Once people could see those results, they became more willing to try it. And it didn’t have to replace everything—we could combine learning with the modeling and control methods people already understood.
